quotes.text: Well, it doesn't feel much like getting back anywhere because we never stopped working. It's just that we haven't done a record in eight years. And that's because, partly, we were having too much fun touring. We've always been a live band anyway. We did start thinking about it four years after "Rapture of the Deep." But what with the declining LP market, there was no real incentive to have the boys leave their families, because we were away a lot already touring and that's kind of precious time. So we put it on the back burner for another year and didn't really know where we were going until Bob Ezrin came to see us when we played Toronto. We had a meeting with him the next day and he gave us a big shot in the arm. He loved what we did onstage and wanted to get into the studio. So that was all we needed. We went back and did the writing session. Then we did the record.

So many things. Decisiveness is one of them. He's clearheaded with a lot of energy. He gets things moving. He'll listen to two or three ideas or suggestions and say, "That's the one." We tend to mull things over for a day or two and have our musical fights. But he kind of circumvented all of that. So we were moving much quicker.
We've had one writing session, been in touch with him and he's excited to go. I think we're going to have another writing session this year and start recording later this year or early next year.

None. It's only after the fact that you can look back and say, "Oh yeah, that's a bit like this was in the past." We never actually sit down and have a meeting saying, "OK, right, what kind of album are we going to make?" Bob was very impressed with the live stuff and wanted to capture what we do live, which is very spontaneous. A few solos were overdubbed. But all the basic rhythm parts, drum parts, bass parts, that's all the four of us in the studio going for it. We used to sort of do things quickly in the studio in the '70s. So if you're looking for a hearkening back, that's the only one I can think of.

The classic-rock thing doesn't really apply anywhere else in the world except the States. We're so categorized in the States that you can't break out of that bubble, whereas most of the places we go, we're just a rock band. Sure, with an illustrious past, but very much a present. And all the hard-core fans know that.

Sure. I like to play. Whatever it is. The Number 1 question I get asked is "Aren't you tired of playing "Smoke on the Water"? No. Why would I get tired of playing a great song that's been wonderful for us? As Steve says, if there were a button at the side of the stage and you could press that button and the audience would go wild, you'd be hard pressed not to press it. But the best songs to play live aren't really that meticulously worked out an arrangement. They're kind of skeletons. I can play different bass lines every night. There are different solos every night. It's always fresh so you never get tired of it. We're like a jazz band more than a rock band in many respects. Of course, we play rock, but there's a lot of real playing going on. It's not just playing parts. It's feeling the moment.

Ian and I differ on that. I had never heard of the band. He says he had, but I'm not sure how true that is. Deep Purple meant nothing in England. In 1968, when "Hush" was a big hit in the States, nothing happened in England. I got turned on to the band just before I joined by the Sweet. Remember the Sweet? Brian Connelly and I were friends. And he said, "Listen to this band, Deep Purple." I said, "Oh, I never heard of them." He said, "They dye their hair black." But the first real impression I got of the band was my audition, which was recording a single. And I was blown away by their musicianship, especially ... well, all of them.

I think it was "Made in Japan." "Made in Japan" was recorded after "Machine Head" and a lot of the material from "Machine Head" was played live. By that time, 1971 or '72, I can't remember, we'd been touring a lot and I think we'd reached a level that that live recording managed to capture. And "Machine Head" was a big hit, sure. But when "Made in Japan" came out, it just went platinum and brought "Machine Head" up with it. That went platinum and "Smoke on the Water" was everywhere. Again, it's back to that live thing. We're players. We don't play parts. Of course, there are certain things you have to work out but there's a lot of free-form going on. We're not a jamming band like Grateful Dead or any of those. It's a different kind of jamming band. It's a hard focus.

It might not be the last record. We've got all of this dead time. We know we can't do any concerts until sometime next year. Now, 10 or 11 months, is a long time for musicians to sit around doing nothing when they could do something. So, it wouldn't surprise me – and I know there's little mutterings going on – that we might get together towards the end of this year and see if we can write some more stuff. If we can, if we've got some ideas that we like, then there's no reason at all why there shouldn't be another record.
Every album we do could be our last album, at this stage, but there was a feeling about this one...

We're a good group of different personalities, and everybody knows their strengths. Something we have that I think is important is how somebody usually notices what nobody else does. In the songwriting process that can be very helpful, but it can also create friction. So we kind of use Bob Ezrin to be the police or judge. He comes in and acts as the final vote. At the end of the day, it works.
